study.design: cross-sectional environmental study with field isolates
study.region_city: Djebel Chekir landfill / Borj Chakir leachate treatment station, Tunis; Oued El Attar river
study.environment: landfill leachate treatment plant (receives some hospital clinical waste) and river receiving the treated leachate
study.source_details: C6: 20 water samples from different steps of the leachate treatment station (young leachate, permeate, raw, concentrate, H2SO4 98% step, ultrafiltration) and from the Oued El Attar river receiving the treated leachate; C. tropicalis isolates came from the river (13) and from the H2SO4 98% treatment step (3)
study.identification_method: Chromogenic medium (CHROMagar Candida), morphology, API Candida / API 20C, MALDI-TOF MS (Bruker)
study.susceptibility_method: Disc diffusion on MHGBM agar (amphotericin B 100 µg disc) and broth microdilution in RPMI 1640 (MIC/MFC, protocol of Noumi et al.)
study.breakpoint_type: author-defined (disc zone: R ≤9 mm, SDD 10–14 mm, S ≥15 mm, attributed to NCCLS endpoints)
study.azole_exposure: not stated (landfill receives municipal and some hospital clinical waste)
study.comments: Only amphotericin B was tested; no azoles. Individual zone diameters and MICs per isolate are reported in Table 1. Table 1 lists 16 C. tropicalis isolates (M2–M57), whereas the text states 17 (46.94%) C. tropicalis and 16 C. krusei; the table lists 17 C. krusei, so the species counts in the text appear to be swapped. The 37 strains in the table include 2 type strains (C. krusei ATCC 6258, C. lusitaniae CECT 11458). Disc categories rely on author-defined cut-offs that are not CLSI breakpoints; the text reports MICs as 'mg/ml' but Table 1 uses µg/ml. Sampling dates are not reported.

resistance.source: river receiving treated landfill leachate (Oued El Attar)
resistance.note: Individual MICs and zone diameters (Table 1); categories from disc diffusion; MICs by broth microdilution (MIC50/MIC90 calculated from the individual MICs). R = M2, M46; SDD = M20, M43.
Individual MICs (M24 0.03, M25 0.03, M36 0.015); all SDD by disc diffusion.

study.design: methodological comparison study with clinical isolates (bloodstream collection)
study.region_city: Collection from the United States; testing at University of Texas–Houston Medical School, Houston, TX
study.environment: clinical isolates (bloodstream) from a US collection; hospitals not specified
study.source_details: C1: bloodstream isolates randomly selected from a US collection
study.susceptibility_method: CLSI broth microdilution (M27-A2), E-test and disc diffusion (M44-A) on glucose–methylene blue Mueller-Hinton agar
study.breakpoint_type: author-defined (arbitrary susceptibility breakpoint ≤1 µg/mL; no clinical breakpoints for posaconazole)
study.comments: Posaconazole only. Only MIC50/MIC90/range per species are reported, with no categorical S/R counts for C. tropicalis. C. tropicalis had the lowest MD–ET concordance (39.0% at 24 h, 70.7% at 48 h; agreement 97.6% and 85.4%), attributed to trailing growth; 3 of the 4 very major errors were C. tropicalis. Collection dates are not reported. Table 1 totals 278 isolates, versus 270 in the text.

resistance.note: No categorical interpretation by species.
48 h is the reading time specified by M27-A2; MIC90 is raised by trailing.

study.region_city: State of Ceará (Fortaleza, Eusébio, Caucaia, Horizonte, Cascavel, Pacatuba, Pacoti)
study.environment: horses housed in stalls and/or paddocks (healthy animals)
study.source_details: C2: nasolacrimal duct of 103 healthy horses; swabs from the duct outlet (18 C. tropicalis) and saline lavage of the duct lumen (2 C. tropicalis)
study.population: healthy horses (11 breeds, juveniles and adults)
study.identification_method: CHROMagar Candida, micromorphology on cornmeal-Tween 80 agar, biochemical tests; VITEK 2 for doubtful cases
study.breakpoint_type: clinical CBP (CLSI M27-S4 for fluconazole and caspofungin); author-defined for itraconazole (R ≥1) and amphotericin B (R >1)
study.azole_exposure: Horses had no previous history of antifungal treatment; the authors hypothesise exposure to azoles used in agricultural practices (not documented).
study.comments: The MIC distribution per C. tropicalis isolate is reported (Table 2). Seven C. tropicalis isolates were resistant to itraconazole only and eight to both fluconazole and itraconazole (15 itraconazole-R, 8 fluconazole-R). Outlet and lumen isolates are not separated in the susceptibility table. Collection dates are not reported. The text contains a typo: the second fluconazole range ('0.03125 to >16') refers to itraconazole.

study.design: cross-sectional (laboratory-based, retrospective collection of clinical isolates)
study.environment: tertiary university hospital (Kahramanmaraş Sütçü İmam University microbiology laboratory); 75.6% of isolates from ICUs
study.source_details: C1: 82 non-albicans isolates from blood (54), urine (25), catheter (1) and wound (2); the source is not given separately for C. tropicalis
study.identification_method: ITS sequencing (ITS1/ITS4, Sanger) as reference; BD Phoenix Yeast ID panel; germ tube and slide culture
study.breakpoint_type: not explicitly stated (presumably EUCAST clinical CBP)
study.comments: C. tropicalis n = 30 by ITS sequencing (26 by Phoenix). Resistance counts by species are taken from the text: amphotericin B 1, fluconazole 9, itraconazole 11, voriconazole 6. The itraconazole species counts (11 C. tropicalis + 9 C. parapsilosis = 20) contradict the stated total of 16; voriconazole and fluconazole totals are consistent. Breakpoints are not specified, and the MIC endpoint was read spectrophotometrically at 24 h. Six C. tropicalis isolates were cross-resistant to at least two triazoles.

study.comments: Single fluconazole-resistant C. tropicalis isolate; MIC values are not reported. Ketoconazole, clotrimazole, posaconazole and amphotericin B were also tested, but results for C. tropicalis are not explicitly given ('fluconazole resistance to C. tropicalis only'). Resistance mechanisms are discussed only from the literature and were not studied. The isolation date is not stated.

study.environment: obstetrics and gynaecology clinics, Authority Al-Gumhorri Hospital
study.source_details: C1: vaginal swabs from 396 symptomatic pregnant women
study.population: pregnant women with symptoms of vaginitis
study.identification_method: HiCrome chromogenic agar, germ tube, API 20C AUX
study.susceptibility_method: disc diffusion (Kirby–Bauer) on Mueller-Hinton agar with 2% glucose and methylene blue (HiMedia discs)
study.standard_document: CLSI (2021) Performance standards for antimicrobial susceptibility testing, 31st ed. (cited)
study.breakpoint_type: author-defined (zone diameters in Table 1; do not correspond to CLSI M44/M60 yeast breakpoints)
study.azole_exposure: not stated (women currently on antimicrobial treatment were excluded; 70.5% had recurrent infection)
study.comments: The standard cited is the CLSI document for bacteria (M100, 31st ed.); the zone breakpoints (e.g. fluconazole S ≥39, R ≤29 mm) are non-standard. Only S/R categories are reported, with no intermediate category and no MICs. Identification is phenotypic. C. tropicalis showed a high voriconazole resistance (63%) with only 7.4% fluconazole resistance, which is implausible and suggests a methodological problem. The miconazole % for C. tropicalis (19.6%) does not match 8/27 (29.6%).

study.design: retrospective cohort / laboratory surveillance of candidaemia episodes
study.environment: tertiary hospital (Hospital Base Valdivia, 505 beds, adult and paediatric ICUs)
study.source_details: C1: blood cultures (first episode per patient)
study.identification_method: CHROMagar Candida, cornmeal-Tween 80 microculture, carbohydrate assimilation, ID-32C; RAPD only for the C. parapsilosis complex
study.susceptibility_method: disc diffusion with Neo-Sensitabs tablets (Rosco) on Mueller-Hinton agar with glucose and methylene blue
study.breakpoint_type: manufacturer criteria (FLC S ≥19, I 15–18, R ≤14 mm; VOR S ≥17, I 14–16, R ≤13 mm); criteria for amphotericin B, itraconazole and caspofungin not stated
study.azole_exposure: not stated (all patients had received broad-spectrum antibiotics)
study.comments: Only 4 C. tropicalis isolates. Disc diffusion is validated only for fluconazole and voriconazole (acknowledged by the authors); the method for itraconazole is not described, although results appear in Table 3. All 4 C. tropicalis were itraconazole SDD and susceptible to the other agents.

resistance.note: Method and criteria for itraconazole are not described in Methods.

study.source_details: C1: clinical specimens from ICU patients; C. tropicalis from urine (11) and catheter (1)
study.identification_method: germ tube, cornmeal-Tween 80 morphology, CHROMagar Candida, API 20C AUX
study.breakpoint_type: clinical CBP (M27-A2 era: fluconazole S ≤8, SDD 16–32, R ≥64)
study.comments: Individual MICs per isolate (Table 1). Under the M27-A2-era breakpoints, 4/12 C. tropicalis were fluconazole SDD (MIC 16–32) and none were R. Under current CLSI breakpoints (S ≤2, SDD 4, R ≥8), 4 would be R and 1 SDD; this was not done by the authors. CT-1 (catheter) and CT-2 (urine) from the same patient were genetically unrelated by RAPD.
